summary: This Wikipedia-based note surveys the Black Death and later plague outbreaks in Europe, Asia and elsewhere, with city-level death tolls from the 15th to 18th centuries. It also covers the scholarly debate over whether bubonic plague caused the Black Death, the genetic evidence identifying Yersinia pestis, and how the term 'Black Death' came into use.
one_line: Overview of Black Death and later plague epidemics in Europe and Asia, the scientific debate over their cause, and the origin of the name.
key_facts: In 1466, perhaps 40,000 people died of the plague in Paris.
Plague epidemics ravaged London in 1563, 1593, 1603, 1625, 1636, and 1665, reducing its population by 10 to 30% during those years.
Over 60% of Norway's population died in 1348–50.
The plague of 1576–77 killed 50,000 in Venice, almost a third of the population.
Epidemics that may have included plague killed an estimated 25 million Chinese and other Asians during the 15 years before it reached Constantinople in 1347.
Nestorian graves dating to 1338–39 near Lake Issyk Kul in Kyrgyzstan have inscriptions referring to plague.
In 1656, the plague killed about half of Naples' 300,000 inhabitants.
Based on genetic evidence from the East Smithfield burial site in England, Schuenemann et al. concluded in 2011 that the Black Death was caused by a variant of Y. pestis that may no longer exist.
Francis Aidan Gasquet wrote about the 'Great Pestilence' in 1893 and implicated rats and fleas in the second edition of 1908.
Gasquet claimed the Latin name atra mors first appeared in modern times in 1631 in a book on Danish history by J.I. Pontanus.
In England, it was not until 1823 that the medieval epidemic was first called the Black Death.
The Paris medical faculty blamed a conjunction of three planets in 1345 for a 'great pestilence in the air'.
According to Geoffrey Parker, 'France alone lost almost a million people to the plague in the epidemic of 1628–31.'
